En un choque a 50 km/h el coche se para: In a crash at 50 km/h the car stops in an instant. With a seat belt you walk away; without it, the same crash can kill you. The difference lies in a few centimetres.

<b>1687</b>Isaac Newton publica sus <i>P: 1687Isaac Newton publishes his Principia with the law of inertia: a body keeps moving in a straight line as long as no force stops it. This is what happens to you inside a car that crashes.
<b>1953</b>El ingeniero estadounidense J: 1953The American engineer John Hetrick patents an "air bag" that inflates in a crash, after a scare in the car with his family.
<b>1959</b>Nils Bohlin, ingeniero de Vol: 1959Nils Bohlin, an engineer at Volvo, designs the three-point seat belt that all cars carry today. Volvo leaves the patent free for any manufacturer to use.
<b>1981</b>Mercedes-Benz monta el airbag: 1981Mercedes-Benz fits the driver's airbag in a production car, the S-Class, always together with the seat belt: the airbag only works well if the belt holds you.
La fuerza que te frena hace un trabajo n: The force that slows you down does negative work that removes all your kinetic energy. The longer the braking distance, the smaller the average force.
Se abre en la pestaña de fuerza variable: It opens in the variable force tab, with a force of −14,700 N over 0.5 m on a 75 kg person travelling at 14 m/s. The work comes out −7350 J and the final speed, zero: the belt stops you exactly in the distance the car crumples.

Un coche va por la ciudad a 50 km/h, uno: A car travels through the city at 50 km/h, about 14 m/s, and crashes head-on into a wall. The car stops in an instant, but what matters is what happens to whoever is inside.\n\nA 75 kg person at that speed has $E_k = ½ m v^2 = ½ · 75 · 14^2 = 7350 "J"$, the same as if they fell from 10 metres high. That energy has to be removed in the crash.

sigues yendo hacia delante aunque el coc: you keep going forward even though the car has already stopped.
Es la primera ley de Newton: un cuerpo s: It is Newton's first law: a body continues in a straight line at the same speed as long as no force stops it. The nose of the car crumples about 50 cm against the wall and the car stops, but nothing stops you.\n\nWithout a seat belt you keep going at 14 m/s until the steering wheel, the dashboard or the windscreen stops you all at once.
Sin cinturón: frenar en 5 centímetros: Without a seat belt: stopping in 5 centimetres
unas 200 veces tu peso, si te paras en s: about 200 times your weight, if you stop in only 5 cm.
El trabajo de la fuerza que te frena tie: The work of the force that stops you has to remove all your kinetic energy: $F · d = ½ m v^2$. If you stop in the distance your chest sinks against the steering wheel, about $d = 5 "cm"$:\n\n$F = {7350}/{0.05} = 147,000 "N"$, about 200 times your weight ($m g = 735 "N"$). No body can withstand that force concentrated on the chest or head.
Con cinturón: frenas con el coche: With seat belt: you brake with the car
unas 20 veces tu peso: diez veces menos,: about 20 times your weight: ten times less, braking over 50 cm.
El cinturón te ata al coche, así que fre: The seat belt ties you to the car, so you brake together with it, while the nose is crushed: about $d = 50 "cm"$. The energy is the same, but the distance is ten times greater:\n\n$F = {7350}/{0.5} = 14,700 "N"$, about 20 times your weight, spread over the pelvis and chest, where the body can withstand it. That is why cars are designed to crumple: the crumple zone is what provides the centimetres.
dura el frenazo del cuerpo sin cinturón: lasts the braking of the body without a seat belt and with seat belt and airbag.
Visto con el impulso, $F · Δt = m · Δv =: Seen with impulse, $F · Δt = m · Δv = 75 · 14 = 1050 "N·s"$ in both cases: what changes is how long it lasts. Braking equally hard the whole time, $Δt = 2d/v$: 7 ms against the steering wheel, 71 ms with the seat belt.\n\nThe airbag inflates in about 30 ms, before you reach the steering wheel, and catches your head and chest with a large, soft surface: it lengthens the time even more and spreads the force. Without a seat belt it is no use: you would arrive before it is full or you would slide out of it.
El cálculo, con el teorema de las fuerza: The calculation, with the work-energy theorem
la fuerza media es inversamente proporci: the average force is inversely proportional to the braking distance.
Todo sale del teorema de las fuerzas viv: It all comes from the work-energy theorem: the work of the force that slows you down is the change in your kinetic energy, $W = −F d = 0 − ½ m v^2$. With double the speed, the force is four times greater; with double the distance, half.\n\nIn Work and energy it opens as a variable force: a force of $−14,700 "N"$ over 0.5 m on a mass of 75 kg travelling at 14 m/s. The area under the graph is $−7350 "J"$ and the final speed comes out zero.
